title: Energy Gap in Solids
short_intro: The energy gap is a forbidden energy range in crystalline solids where no electron quantum states can exist. Its magnitude determines whether a material acts as an insulator, semiconductor, or conductor.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of energy gap, distinction between conductors, semiconductors, and insulators based on energy bands, effect of temperature on electrical conductivity, and basic valence and conduction band concepts.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Band theory of solids using Bloch theorem and Kronig-Penney model, direct and indirect band gaps, temperature dependence of Fermi level, and effective mass of electrons.

prerequisites: Wave-particle duality and de Broglie wavelength

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Energy Bands and Gap
bullets: In isolated atoms, electrons occupy discrete energy levels governed by quantum numbers.
When atoms are brought together to form a crystal lattice, interatomic interactions split these discrete levels into closely spaced continuous bands.
The forbidden region between the valence band and the conduction band is known as the energy gap (E<sub>g</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Classification of Materials
bullets: Insulators possess a very large energy gap (E<sub>g</sub> > 3 eV), preventing thermal excitation of electrons from the valence to the conduction band.
Semiconductors have a moderate energy gap (E<sub>g</sub> &approx; 0.1 eV to 3 eV), allowing limited carrier excitation at room temperature.
Conductors (metals) have either an overlapping valence and conduction band or a partially filled band with zero energy gap.

concept_notes.heading: Direct and Indirect Band Gaps
bullets: In a direct band gap semiconductor, the minimum of the conduction band and the maximum of the valence band occur at the same crystal momentum (k = 0).
In an indirect band gap semiconductor, the conduction band minimum and valence band maximum occur at different crystal momenta.
Direct band gap materials (e.g., GaAs) efficiently emit photons, making them suitable for optoelectronic devices.

concept_notes.heading: Temperature Dependence of Energy Gap
bullets: The energy gap of semiconductors decreases with an increase in temperature due to thermal expansion of the lattice and increased atomic vibrations.
Empirically expressed as E<sub>g</sub>(T) = E<sub>g</sub>(0) - \frac{\alpha T^2}{T + \beta}, where \alpha and \beta are material constants.
This reduction allows higher intrinsic carrier concentration at elevated temperatures.

derivations.title: Intrinsic Carrier Concentration and Energy Gap
derivations.conditions: Non-degenerate intrinsic semiconductor with parabolic bands
steps: Express the electron concentration in the conduction band as n = N<sub>c</sub> exp(-(E<sub>c</sub> - E<sub>f</sub>)/kT).
Express the hole concentration in the valence band as p = N<sub>v</sub> exp(-(E<sub>f</sub> - E<sub>v</sub>)/kT).
Use the mass-action law for intrinsic semiconductors where n = p = n<sub>i</sub>, leading to n<sub>i<sup>2</sup><sub> = N<sub>c</sub>N<sub>v</sub> exp(-E<sub>g</sub>/kT).
Take the natural logarithm to relate the band gap to the temperature variation of the intrinsic carrier concentration.

derivations.title: Band Gap Determination from Conductivity Measurements
derivations.conditions: Intrinsic semiconductor operating in the thermal excitation region
steps: Write electrical conductivity as \sigma \approx e(\mu_n n + \mu_p p) \approx e \mu n_i.
Substitute the temperature dependence of intrinsic carrier concentration: \sigma = \sigma_0 \exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right).
Take natural logarithms on both sides: \ln \sigma = \ln \sigma_0 - \frac{E_g}{2kT}.
Plot \ln \sigma versus 1/T to obtain a straight line whose slope yields the energy gap.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Band Diagrams for Solids
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three vertical columns showing Insulator (large gap between valence and conduction bands), Semiconductor (small gap), and Conductor (overlapping or half-filled bands).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Clearly displays the magnitude of the forbidden energy gap which dictates the macroscopic electrical behavior of the material.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in TGT/PGT matching and identification questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Four-Probe Method / Conductivity vs Temperature Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of ln(\sigma) on the y-axis against 1000/T (K<sup>-1</sup>) on the x-axis, showing a linear negative slope in the intrinsic region.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the straight-line portion directly yields the activation energy, which corresponds to half of the band gap (E<sub>g</sub>/2).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problem formulation and experimental principle verification in PGT physics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Optical Absorption Coefficient vs Photon Energy
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting absorption coefficient (α<sup>2</sup> or α) against photon energy (hν), showing a sharp rise starting at hν = E<sub>g</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The intercept of the linear extrapolation on the energy axis gives the direct band gap value of the semiconductor.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in advanced PGT conceptual questions regarding optical characterization.

solved_numericals.question: The energy gap of germanium is approximately 0.72 eV. Calculate the maximum wavelength of a photon that can excite an electron from the valence band to the conduction band in germanium.
solution_steps: Substitute constants: h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}, c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}.

solved_numericals.question: The electrical conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor doubles when its temperature is raised from 300 K to 330 K. Assuming the band gap remains constant over this temperature range, determine the energy gap E_g.
solution_steps: At T_1 = 300 K, \sigma_1 = C \exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT_1}\right); at T_2 = 330 K, \sigma_2 = C \exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT_2}\right).
Substitute values: k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5} \text{ eV/K}, T_1 = 300, T_2 = 330.

solved_numericals.question: Find the threshold frequency of light for photoelectric-like interband absorption in a semiconductor with a band gap of 1.2 eV.
solution_steps: Substitute Planck's constant h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}.

assumptions_and_limitations: The Kronig-Penney model assumes an idealized 1D periodic rectangular potential, which is a simplification of actual 3D atomic potentials.
Effective mass approximation assumes electrons remain close to the band extrema where the E-k dispersion relation can be approximated as parabolic.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Electrons flow freely inside the forbidden energy gap.
common_misconceptions.correct: No electronic energy states exist within the energy gap, so electrons cannot occupy or travel through energy levels in this range.
common_misconceptions.why: Quantum mechanical solutions to the periodic potential yield zero probability density for states inside the forbidden band.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The energy gap increases with an increase in temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: The energy gap decreases as temperature increases.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal expansion and increased lattice vibrations broaden the interatomic spacing fluctuations, reducing the crystal potential amplitude and narrowing the band gap.

quick_revision: Energy gap is the forbidden energy zone separating valence and conduction bands.
Insulators have E<sub>g</sub> > 3 eV, semiconductors have 0.1 eV < E<sub>g</sub> < 3 eV, and conductors have E<sub>g</sub> = 0.
Intrinsic carrier concentration depends exponentially on -E<sub>g</sub>/(2kT).
Semiconductor band gap decreases monotonically with increasing temperature.
